messages.subject: Optimize a generalized linear mixed model with known covariance matrix
parts:
Hi Stan group,

I am building an ordered categorical model with a random effect. The model can be written as: f(y) ~ x * beta + u, where u ~ (0, sigma * K), and K as a covariance matrix is known. The model as attached below is running fine but very slow. It takes hours for a 2000 iteration run. Could you please give me your suggestions to speed things up?

Secondly, in a separate model with an additional predictor, is it possible to reuse the estimation of the random effect u? I have to include thousands of genetic variants, means there will be thousands of run. So, speed and efficiency is important to me.

Thanks,

//--- The model
data {
  int<lower=1> N;  // Sample number
  int<lower=1> K;  // Response categories
  matrix[N,N] KS;  // Covariate matrix
  int<lower=1,upper=K> Ad[N];  // Response
  int<lower=1,upper=2> Sex[N];  //  M:F
}

transformed data {
  matrix[N,N] CK;  // Cholesky K
  vector[N] mu;  // 0
  vector[N] sexF;  // Relative to M

  CK <- cholesky_decompose(KS);

  for (i in 1:N) {
    mu[i] <- 0;
    sexF[i]  <- Sex[i]  == 2;
  }
}

parameters {
  vector[N] u;  // ramdom effect
  real<lower=0> sigmaU;

  real pSex;  // Female

  positive_ordered[K-1] cut;  // cut points
}

model {
  vector[N] yhat;

  pSex ~ normal(0, 5);
  sigmaU ~ normal(0, 5);

  u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, sigmaU * CK);

  yhat <- u + sexF * pSex;

  for (n in 1:N)
    Ad[n] ~ ordered_logistic(yhat[n], cut);
}

Hi Ben,

Thanks for your reply. I have taken your suggestions, but put the random effect u as a local variable in the model block, instead of a transformed parameter, so the sampling process would not need to store u every step. I have attached my new code below.

The speed has significantly increased with your trick, but I found it is still not satisfying. I found the matrix operation u<- sigmaU * (CK * z) really slow things down, in an order. If CK matrix was dropped in u <- sigmaU * (CK * z), it is much more quicker. I assume this is only an explicit assignment operation which will only be executed once each sampling step. vector[N] u;  // random effect
pAge ~ normal(0, 5);

It's not the assignment that's expensive, it's
propagating all the partial derivatives that are entailed.

In your case, it's not even that bad, because you have
a data matrix multiplied by a parameter vector, and derivatives
only propagate through parameters.

Also, the evaluation happens each leapfrog step within each
iteration. So you can look at the number of steps taken in
the output each iteration and it's really that many evaluations
you're doing.

- Bob

parts:
The main problem is that you can't fit hierarchical models with
optimization unless you are very careful with priors (see Gelman et al.'s
papers on this topic).

The second problem is that we only compute the log density up to a constant
normalizing term, and it includes the prior as well as the likelihood,
so you can't directly compare log likelihoods this way. You could compute
the log likelihood in your model if you want, say in generated quantities.
If you use the functional forms (e.g. normal_log(y,mu,sigma) instead of
the sampling notation form y ~ normal(mu,sigma)), we include all the normalizing
terms.

- Bob

On Monday, October 27, 2014 11:31:16 AM UTC-4, Xulong Wang wrote:
I am building an ordered categorical model with a random effect. The model can be written as: f(y) ~ x * beta + u, where u ~ (0, sigma * K), and K as a covariance matrix is known. The model as attached below is running fine but very slow. It takes hours for a 2000 iteration run. Could you please give me your suggestions to speed things up?

Yes, see edits to your model below. Basically, it comes down to the rule to not use any of the variants of multi_normal() unless the left-hand side is data.
 
Secondly, in a separate model with an additional predictor, is it possible to reuse the estimation of the random effect u? I have to include thousands of genetic variants, means there will be thousands of run. So, speed and efficiency is important to me.

If I understand you correctly, you cannot do so in a theoretically satisfying way. This is similar to the discussion of the cut() function in the BUGS family of software.
 
//--- The model
data {
  int<lower=1> N;  // Sample number
  int<lower=1> K;  // Response categories
  matrix[N,N] KS;  // Covariate matrix
  int<lower=1,upper=K> Ad[N];  // Response
  int<lower=1,upper=2> Sex[N];  //  M:F
}

transformed data {
  matrix[N,N] CK;  // Cholesky K
  # vector[N] mu;  // 0 (not needed anymore)
  vector[N] sexF;  // Relative to M

  CK <- cholesky_decompose(KS);

  for (i in 1:N) {
    # mu[i] <- 0; // not needed anymore
    sexF[i]  <- Sex[i]  == 2;
  }
}

parameters {
  #vector[N] u;  // random effect
      vector[N] z; // primative of random effect
  real<lower=0> sigmaU;

  real pSex;  // Female

  positive_ordered[K-1] cut;  // cut points
}
transformed data {
      vector[N] u;
      u <- sigmaU * (CK * z);
    }
model {
  vector[N] yhat;

  pSex ~ normal(0, 5);
  sigmaU ~ normal(0, 5);

  #u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, sigmaU * CK);
      z <- normal(0,1); // implies u ~ multi_normal()

  yhat <- u + sexF * pSex;

  for (n in 1:N)
    Ad[n] ~ ordered_logistic(yhat[n], cut);
}
